items.prompt: Which command creates a brand-new commit that cancels an older one?
items.explanation: revert adds a new commit whose changes are the inverse of the old one; history only grows.

items.prompt: Which command moves the branch pointer backward?
items.explanation: reset repoints the branch label at an earlier commit.

items.prompt: Which of these never changes history at all?
items.explanation: checkout only moves your working position or restores files; it neither rewrites nor adds commits.

items.prompt: Which statement describes a command that 'rewrites history'?
choices: It adds one more commit on top
It prints the log in a different order
It copies files into a new folder
It moves a branch back so some commits are no longer reachable
items.explanation: Rewriting means commits that were reachable from the branch no longer are.

items.prompt: Which command only ever adds to history?
items.explanation: revert is append-only; every reset variant moves the pointer.

items.prompt: 'Undo' in casual speech maps to how many distinct Git behaviors in this unit?
choices: One, they are all the same
Two, only reset and revert exist
items.explanation: Each verb targets a different thing, so the word 'undo' hides the choice.

items.prompt: Which kind of undo is most dangerous when other people share the branch?
choices: One that adds a new commit
One that restores a single file
items.explanation: Rewritten history that others already pulled will disagree with their copies.

items.prompt: You want to look at an old commit without changing any branch. Which verb family fits?
items.explanation: Moving HEAD to look around is checkout's job and rewrites nothing.

items.prompt: A teammate says: 'revert and reset both undo a commit, so it does not matter which I use.' What is the most important thing that claim misses?
choices: Reset is always faster than revert, so it should be preferred whenever you need to undo something
Revert cannot undo commits that are older than a day, while reset can reach any commit
Reset rewrites the branch's history, revert only adds to it; that matters on shared branches
Reset only works on individual files while revert works on whole commits and branches
items.explanation: Both cancel the effect, but only reset changes what the branch says happened, so only reset can make a shared copy diverge.
items.reference:
Same word, three targets
🔀 checkout: move HEAD, or restore files
⏪ revert: add a commit that cancels an old one
⚠️ reset: move the branch pointer back
Why: "undo" is three different questions: where am I, what does the branch say, what do my files look like.
items.learnMore:
Rewriting vs. adding

Only reset rewrites what a branch says happened. Revert appends; checkout never touches history at all. The moment a branch is shared, that difference decides who gets conflicts.

Common mistake

Treating the three verbs as synonyms because casual speech calls them all "undo".
items.reflection: Think of undoing a mistake in a shared document: deleting your text, adding a correction below it, and restoring last Tuesday's version are three different acts. Which one would you use if colleagues had already read the page?

items.prompt: After an undo command, 'git log' no longer shows the mistaken commit anywhere on the branch. Which verb was most likely used?
choices: revert, because it deletes the commit from the branch and leaves only the new commit
checkout, because it removes bad commits from the log when given a hash
restore, because it rewrites the log to match the files on disk
reset, because it moved the branch pointer behind the commit
items.explanation: Revert leaves the commit visible and adds another; only a pointer move hides it from the branch.

choices: revert, since it can target any commit and add a new one without disturbing the rest
reset, since it can remove just that one commit from the middle without touching newer ones
checkout, since it can delete a commit by its hash from anywhere in the branch
restore, since it can drop any commit as long as the file paths are listed
items.explanation: Reset can only drop commits from the tip backward; revert cancels one commit anywhere in history.

items.prompt: What does 'git checkout .' do in the scenario?
choices: Reverts only the file you edited last
Reverts every uncommitted change in the current directory
Creates a backup of the directory
items.explanation: The dot means the whole current directory, so every uncommitted change was wiped.

items.prompt: What is the first command in the emergency checklist?
items.explanation: Reading status shows which files are at risk before anything is discarded.

items.prompt: Which command restores only config.json?
items.explanation: Naming the exact file is what narrows the scope.

items.prompt: Does 'git checkout -- .' limit the restore to one file?
choices: Yes, the double dash narrows it
No, it still covers everything under the directory
Yes, it only affects staged files
No, it only affects new files
items.explanation: The -- only marks that a path follows; the dot is still the whole directory.

items.prompt: If you do not understand the git status output, what does the checklist say?
choices: Delete the file and re-create it
items.explanation: Unclear status means unclear risk, so skip the broad commands.

items.prompt: The mistake is already pushed to the shared branch. What does the checklist prefer?
items.explanation: Shared history should only be added to, which revert does.

items.prompt: What was lost in the scenario?
choices: Three hours of uncommitted feature.js work
items.explanation: Uncommitted edits are not stored in any commit, so the restore overwrote them.

items.prompt: Who warned you before the whole-directory restore ran?
choices: Nobody, there is no confirmation prompt
items.explanation: checkout with a path discards changes silently.

items.prompt: You run 'git status' and see config.json and feature.js both modified. You only want to drop the change to config.json. Which command is both correct and safest?
choices: git checkout -- . (restores everything under the directory)
git reset --hard (restores everything, including staged work)
git checkout . (restores every uncommitted change here)
items.explanation: Only the named path is restored, leaving feature.js alone.
items.reference:
Scope is part of the command
🎯 checkout -- config.json: one file
💥 checkout .: every file under this directory
🩺 git status first: see what is at risk
Why: the same verb with a different path can be harmless or destroy hours of work.
items.learnMore:
Read the scope before you press Enter

A dot means "everything here". The double dash only marks the end of options, it does not narrow the scope. Naming the exact file is what narrows it.

Common mistake

Believing that adding -- makes a whole-directory restore safe.
items.reflection: Where else does a small wildcard or 'select all' turn a precise action into a sweeping one, like emptying a whole folder when you meant one file? What habit would make you check the scope first?

items.prompt: A colleague proposes 'git checkout -- .' as the safe version of 'git checkout .' because it has the double dash. What is wrong with that?
choices: The double dash makes the command destructive for staged files only
The double dash only marks a path follows; the dot still means the whole directory
It only works for untracked files, which is why it feels safer to use
It asks for confirmation before running, which just makes it slower
items.explanation: Scope comes from the path, not from the --.

items.prompt: Which of these is NOT one of the three places Git keeps state?
items.explanation: Git's local state chain is commits, index, working tree.

items.prompt: What is the index?
choices: The staging area: changes prepared for the next commit
A compressed copy of the repository
items.explanation: The index holds what will go into the next commit.

items.prompt: What is the working tree?
choices: The actual files on disk, including uncommitted edits
items.explanation: It is what you see and edit in your folder.

items.prompt: Which command moves the branch pointer but leaves index and files alone?
items.explanation: --soft stops after the pointer move.

items.prompt: Which reset mode overwrites files on disk?
items.explanation: Only --hard reaches the working tree.

items.prompt: What does revert do to history?
choices: Rewrites the old commit in place
Adds a new commit; nothing is moved backward
items.explanation: Revert is append-only.

items.prompt: What is the reflog?
choices: A local diary of where HEAD and branches recently moved
The list of files in the index
A backup of the working tree
items.explanation: It records pointer movements, not file contents.

items.prompt: Which command changes only the file you name?
items.explanation: A path-scoped checkout touches just that path in the working tree.

items.prompt: You ran 'git reset --soft HEAD~1'. What state are you in?
choices: The last commit is gone and its changes are deleted from the working tree
The last commit remains on the branch and its changes are now unstaged
The last commit is gone from the branch, but its changes remain staged
Nothing changed because --soft is a dry run that only prints what would happen
items.explanation: --soft moves only the pointer; index and files keep the changes.
items.reference:
Three places state lives
📌 Commits: branch pointer and HEAD
🗂️ Index: what is staged
📄 Working tree: files on disk
Why: every undo command is defined by how far along this chain it reaches.

Both overwrite files on disk, and --hard additionally deletes the repository
Only --mixed touches the index; --hard leaves the staging area alone
They are identical except that --hard runs faster on large repositories
items.explanation: Each mode is a superset of the previous one; --hard adds the working tree.

items.explanation: A branch name argument means switching branches.

items.prompt: 'git checkout a1b2c3d' with a commit hash does what?
choices: Moves HEAD to that commit, detached from any branch
items.explanation: Checking out a hash gives a detached HEAD.

items.prompt: 'git checkout -- app.js' does what?
choices: Switches to a branch called app.js
items.explanation: A path after -- means restore that file.

items.prompt: What is the modern command for switching branches?
items.explanation: switch covers branch and commit moves.

items.prompt: What is the modern command for restoring files?
items.explanation: restore handles file content only.

items.prompt: Which Git version introduced switch and restore?
items.explanation: They were added in Git 2.23.

items.prompt: What does checkout NOT do to history?
items.explanation: checkout never changes the commit graph.

items.prompt: What decides which of checkout's behaviors runs?
items.explanation: The same word does three different things based on the argument.

items.prompt: You typed 'git checkout 9f2e1ab' and then made two commits. You run 'git switch main'. What happens to your two commits?
choices: They are reachable from no branch and can be lost unless you attach one
They are merged into main automatically when you switch away from the detached HEAD
They are reverted by Git so that main stays clean and consistent
They move to a new branch that Git names after the commit hash
items.explanation: A detached HEAD has no branch to keep the commits reachable.
items.reference:
The argument decides
🌿 branch name: switch branches
🔗 commit hash: detached HEAD
📄 -- path: restore files
Why: one verb, three shapes; switch and restore split them apart.

Why Git 2.23 split the verb

switch only moves HEAD; restore only touches file contents. Neither can be argument-confused into the other, which a bare checkout can.

Common mistake

Assuming a detached HEAD has a branch that will keep new commits safe.

switch only moves HEAD and never restores file contents
switch refuses any argument that contains a dot, so a sweeping path is impossible
switch works only on staged files, so unstaged edits can never be touched
items.explanation: The split verbs have disjoint jobs, so a path cannot be mistaken for a destructive restore.

items.prompt: Which reset mode is the default?
items.explanation: Bare 'git reset <commit>' uses --mixed.

items.prompt: Which mode leaves staged changes staged?
items.explanation: --soft touches only the pointer.

items.prompt: Which mode unstages but keeps the file edits on disk?
items.explanation: --mixed resets the index only.

items.prompt: Which mode can discard uncommitted work with no prompt?
items.explanation: --hard overwrites the working tree silently.

items.prompt: Do all three modes move the branch pointer?
items.explanation: Moving the pointer is the shared first step.

items.prompt: Which mode is handy to squash recent commits into one?
items.explanation: After --soft the changes are still staged, ready to commit as one.

items.prompt: How many layers does --hard touch?
items.explanation: Pointer, index, and working tree.

items.prompt: Which mode is the most dangerous?
items.explanation: Only --hard can lose uncommitted work.

items.prompt: You made three commits locally and want them back as uncommitted edits, still staged, ready to recommit as one. Which command fits?
choices: git reset --hard HEAD~3 (changes become unstaged edits)
git revert HEAD~3 (adds one commit canceling the third)
git checkout HEAD~3 (moves to a detached HEAD there)
items.explanation: --soft moves the pointer back while keeping index and files intact.
items.reference:
How far each mode reaches
1️⃣ --soft: pointer only
2️⃣ --mixed (default): pointer and index
3️⃣ --hard: pointer, index, and files
Why: each mode is a superset of the last; only --hard can destroy uncommitted work.
items.learnMore:
Safe to your files is not safe to shared history

All three modes move the branch pointer, so all three rewrite history. The mode only decides what happens to your local files.

Common mistake

Thinking --mixed is safe to run on commits teammates have already pulled.

items.prompt: A teammate says --mixed is 'safe' because it never touches files. When is that reasoning still dangerous?
choices: Whenever the files are binary, because the pointer cannot move past them
Whenever the index is empty, because then --mixed has nothing to reset
Never, because --mixed is always safe for every kind of history
When the commits being moved past were already pulled by others, since the pointer move still rewrites shared history
items.explanation: File safety and history safety are separate guarantees.

items.explanation: Revert adds history instead of rewriting shared history.

choices: The inverse of the reverted commit's changes
A copy of the old commit
items.explanation: Its diff is the exact inverse.

items.prompt: After a revert, is the original mistake still in the log?
items.explanation: Revert never removes anything.

items.prompt: What is the main cost of reset plus force-push on shared history?
choices: Teammates' histories diverge and need manual reconciliation
items.explanation: Their copies include commits the rewritten branch no longer has.

items.prompt: The one exception that allows reset on shared history is...
choices: The team explicitly agrees and re-syncs
items.explanation: A coordinated rewrite is the rare exception.

items.prompt: Which decision question matters most?
choices: How scary does the command look?
Has anyone else possibly already seen this commit?
How long did the commit take?
items.explanation: Sharing, not scariness, decides rewrite versus add.

items.prompt: Does revert's cleanup cost grow with the number of teammates who pulled?
items.explanation: Nothing they hold is rewritten.

items.prompt: A broken commit was pushed ten minutes ago and three teammates have already pulled it. What is the best way to undo it?
choices: git revert the commit and push the new commit
git reset --hard before it and force-push to the shared branch
git checkout the previous commit and push from that detached HEAD
Delete the remote branch and recreate it from your local copy
items.explanation: Revert adds a normal commit teammates can pull without conflict.
items.reference:
One deciding question
🙋 Only mine, never pushed: reset is fine
👥 Others may have it: revert
🤝 Agreed rewrite: reset + force-push
Why: revert adds history; reset rewrites it, and rewritten shared history diverges from everyone else's copy.
items.learnMore:
Cost grows with teammates

A reset plus force-push costs cleanup time for every person who already pulled. A revert costs the same no matter how many have it.

Common mistake

Choosing reset because it is one step, without asking who else has the commit.

items.prompt: Why should you only practice reset --hard in a throwaway repo?
choices: It can delete uncommitted work without a prompt
items.explanation: No prompt, no undo for uncommitted work.

items.prompt: What happens to old commits after reset moves the pointer past them?
choices: They are pushed to the remote
They stay in the object store until garbage collected
items.explanation: Unreachable is not the same as deleted.

items.prompt: Which habit prevents most reset --hard disasters?
items.explanation: Status reveals uncommitted work at risk.

items.prompt: You had one committed file and one staged, never-committed file when you ran reset --hard HEAD~1. Which statement is correct?
choices: Both can be recovered through the reflog because both were present before the reset
The committed file can be found through the reflog; the staged file is gone
Neither can be recovered, since reset --hard erases everything it touches
Only the staged file can be recovered, because staging stores a copy of it
items.explanation: Only content captured in a commit leaves a trail.
items.reference:
Was it ever committed?
✅ Committed once: reflog can bring it back
❌ Only staged or untracked: gone for good
📓 Reflog records pointer moves, not file contents
Why: recoverability depends on a commit having captured the content, not on how scary the command looked.
items.learnMore:
What the reflog can and cannot see

Every commit is an object that keeps its file contents. Moving a pointer past it leaves the object in place, so reflog entries can point back. A file never committed has no object at all.

Common mistake

Assuming the reflog is a general file-recovery tool.
items.reflection: Where do you rely on a save point (a commit, a backup, a version history) without noticing, and what work in your life lives only in the unsaved state right now?

items.prompt: A teammate says 'git reflog will save any work I lose.' What is the best correction?
choices: It only works on the remote, so local losses are never covered by it
It expires after one minute, so it only helps with very recent mistakes
It only tracks branch names, never the commits those branches pointed to
It only recovers commits, so uncommitted edits are not covered
items.explanation: The reflog records pointer positions, not working-tree contents.

items.prompt: You are about to run reset --hard and are unsure whether you have uncommitted work. What is the best low-cost safeguard?
choices: Commit the work first, even to a throwaway commit, so a reflog entry exists
Run the reset with --force so that Git keeps a backup of the working tree
Run the reset twice, since the second pass restores what the first removed
Switch to the remote branch first, which copies local edits over automatically
items.explanation: A commit turns unrecoverable content into recoverable content.

items.prompt: After 'git revert c3d4e5f', is c3d4e5f still in the log?
items.explanation: Revert appends; it never removes.

items.prompt: What does a teammate who already pulled the bad commit receive after your revert?
choices: A merge conflict on every file
items.explanation: The revert commit arrives like any other commit.

items.prompt: Why does revert not cause diverged history?
items.explanation: Existing commits keep their hashes.

items.prompt: What does 'fixed' mean after a revert?
choices: The bug commit no longer exists
The current files no longer contain the bug
items.explanation: The state is fixed; the commit remains.

items.prompt: After reset to before the mistake, what do commits after the mistake become locally?
items.explanation: They are unreachable from the branch.

items.prompt: Which approach leaves the mistake visible in the log?
items.explanation: Only revert keeps it.

items.prompt: In a gitGraph, where does the revert commit appear?
choices: On top of the existing commits
items.explanation: It is appended to the branch tip.

items.prompt: Why is revert 'append-only'?
choices: It only adds a commit and never moves the pointer back
items.explanation: No existing commit changes.

items.prompt: Two teammates pulled the bad commit; you revert it and push. What do they do to catch up?
choices: A force-reset to the remote, discarding their local copy of the bad commit
Delete their clone and fetch everything again from the remote
A rebase onto the old commit so their history matches the rewritten one
A normal pull, receiving the revert commit as one more commit
items.explanation: Nothing they hold was rewritten, so no special handling is needed.
items.reference:
What a teammate sees
🟢 revert: one extra commit arrives normally
🔴 reset + force-push: history no longer matches theirs
👀 Mistake stays in the log after a revert
Why: revert never rewrites commits that others already hold.
items.learnMore:
Fixed does not mean erased

After a revert the broken commit is still visible, checkoutable, and diffable. What changes is that the current file state no longer has the bug.

Common mistake

Expecting the log to look like the mistake never happened after a revert.
items.reflection: Think of a published correction in a newspaper versus a silently edited article. Which builds more trust with readers who already saw the original, and when would silent editing be acceptable?

items.prompt: A reviewer sees the broken commit and its revert both in git log and asks if the cleanup failed. How do you answer?
choices: No, revert fixes the file state while keeping history append-only, which is the point on shared branches
Yes, and you should rewrite history to hide both commits from the log
Yes, the revert was applied to the wrong commit and needs redoing
No, Git automatically hides reverted commits once the revert is pushed
items.explanation: Visibility of the mistake is by design.

items.prompt: Compare what happens to commits made after the mistake: reset to before it versus revert of it.
choices: Revert orphans them, reset keeps them
Reset orphans them locally; revert leaves them in place
items.explanation: Reset moves the branch behind them; revert adds a commit on top of them.

items.prompt: Mistake only in one file in the working tree. Best command?
items.explanation: File-scoped restore touches only that file.

items.prompt: Bad commit never pushed. Best command?
items.explanation: Nobody else has it, so rewriting is fine.

items.prompt: Bad commit pushed and pulled by others. Best command?
items.explanation: Add history rather than rewriting shared history.

items.prompt: After 'git checkout <hash>' you commit twice. What is the risk?
choices: Those commits belong to no branch
items.explanation: A detached HEAD has no branch keeping commits reachable.

items.prompt: What is wrong with a silent force-push after a reset?
choices: Teammates get divergent-history errors they do not understand
items.explanation: Others pull next and find their history no longer matches.

items.prompt: What does revert on a never-pushed commit leave behind?
choices: A confusing revert pair in history
items.explanation: A clean reset would have removed it.

items.prompt: What should you run before any command that could discard state?
items.explanation: It shows what is at risk.

items.prompt: Which situation allows reset plus force-push?
choices: The team explicitly agreed to rewrite
items.explanation: Coordination is the only exception.

items.prompt: You spent an hour committing on a detached HEAD, then switched to main. What is the right next step if you want to keep that work?
choices: Run git revert on main so the detached commits are cancelled out
Find the commit via reflog and attach a branch to it
Run reset --hard origin/main, which pulls the detached commits back in
Delete the branch and re-clone, since detached commits sync from the remote
items.explanation: The commits are unreachable but still in the object store; a new branch makes them reachable.
items.reference:
Pick the right row
📄 One file in working tree: restore
🙋 Local bad commit: reset
👥 Pushed and pulled: revert
🤝 Agreed rewrite: reset + coordinated force-push
Why: each failure mode is a way of skipping one of these rows.
items.learnMore:
Four ways undo goes wrong

Skipping git status, force-pushing silently, committing on a detached HEAD, and using revert on a commit nobody has seen. Each applies the right tool to the wrong situation.

Common mistake

Using one favorite undo command for every situation.
items.reflection: Which of your own habits, like a favorite shortcut or a one-size-fits-all fix, would you want to turn into a quick checklist before using it in a high-stakes moment?

items.prompt: A coworker never pushed a typo commit and uses revert to fix it. What is the downside?
choices: The typo remains in the files, because revert only changes history
The remote is corrupted, because revert on local commits cannot be pushed
History gets an unnecessary revert pair that a clean reset would have avoided
Teammates must re-clone, because reverts always change existing hashes
items.explanation: Revert's safety only matters once sharing is in play.

items.prompt: Your team agreed to rewrite a shared branch. Which step is easiest to forget and causes the most confusion?
choices: Running git gc afterwards to clean unreachable objects from every clone
Renaming the branch so the rewritten history has a fresh, distinct name
Deleting old tags on the remote so they do not point at removed commits
Telling everyone to re-sync their local clones to the new tip
items.explanation: A silent force-push relocates the confusion to whoever pulls next.
